power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: Sample size was determined a priori via Monte Carlo power simulation targeting H2 (the effect of expression valence on WTP). Because no prior estimate was available, simulations were based on synthetic data with a smallest effect of interest of 0.5 pence (WTP difference between happy and neutral expressions), and we targeted the conventional 80% power. The simulation model included random intercepts for participant and demonstrator, as preregistered (see Supplementary Materials for details). With 1,000 iterations per candidate sample size, simulations indicated that N = 400 participants would yield approximately 80% power to detect this effect at α = .05. We recruited 420 participants to account for potential exclusions.
table.header: Method Participants
table.effect_size_metric_other: WTP difference in pence between happy and neutral expressions

table.text: Sample size was determined a priori via Monte Carlo power simulation (1,000 iterations per candidate sample size) for the H4 interaction (expression valence × group membership on WTP), based on a pilot study with the same design (N = 419; see Supplementary Materials). The target effect was the pilot estimate of this interaction (b = 0.29 pence). We targeted 90% rather than 80% power to buffer against imprecise pilot estimates. Simulations indicated that N = 1,060 participants would yield approximately 90% power to detect this effect at α = .05. We planned to recruit 1,166 participants to account for potential exclusions; due to minor over-recruitment on Prolific, 1,168 participants took part.
table.header: Method Participants
table.statistical_test_other: H4 interaction (expression valence × group membership on WTP)

table.text: Sample size was determined a priori by simulation (1,000 simulations per specification) for the expression valence [happy] × group membership [in-group] interaction on WTP (H4), using variance components from a pilot sample (N = 97 after exclusions). To guard against overestimating this effect, we used a conservative estimate following Perugini et al. (2014), namely the lower bound of the 60% confidence interval of the Experiment 2 estimate under its preregistered random-effects structure (b = 0.23 pence, SE = 0.09), rescaled to the payout range of Experiment 3 (b = 0.19 pence). With N = 1,400 after exclusions, power for this effect was 84%-90% under the random-effects structures supported by the pilot data, and above 90% for the Experiment 2 point estimate (see Supplementary Materials, Table S6). We planned to recruit 1,490 participants to account for an expected exclusion rate of 6%; due to minor over-recruitment on Prolific, 1,508 participants took part.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("p < .20", "ps ≥ .085", "ps > .970", 
"ps ≥ .25"), Text = c("In all experiments, random-effects structures were selected by, starting from the most complex candidate structure, simplifying the structure until it converged, was not singular, and fit the data better than the next simpler structure (likelihood-ratio test, p < .20; Matuschek et al., 2017).", 
"Across expressions, in-group demonstrators were inferred to feel 1.50 rating points better (p < .001; see H3), and this difference did not differ significantly between any two expressions (all ps ≥ .085; see H3; angry: aG = 1.75, neutral: aG = 0.75, happy: aG = 1.99; Figure 6D).", 
"The weighting did not differ between any two expressions (all |t| < 0.04, ps > .970) and was not significant for any expression on its own (all ps ≥ .25; Table S12).", 
"The weighting did not differ between any two expressions (all |t| < 0.04, ps > .970) and was not significant for any expression on its own (all ps ≥ .25; Table S12)."
)), row.names = c(NA, -4L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"
))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. table.formatted: In all experiments, random-effects structures were selected by, starting from the most complex candidate structure, simplifying the structure until it converged, was not singular, and fit the data better than the next simpler structure (likelihood-ratio test, p < .20; <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Matuschek et al., 2017)</ref>.
table.header: Analysis

table.header: Can Inferred Affect Account for the Expression Effect on WTP?
table.expanded: The relationship between inferred affect and WTP did not differ between neutral and happy expressions, binteraction = 0.0050, SE = 0.0063, 95% CI [-0.0074, 0.0175], t(614) = 0.79, p = .430.

table.header: H3 | Expressions From In-Group Members Are Rated as Reflecting More Positive Feelings Than Expressions From Out-Group Members
table.expanded: The in-group effect did not differ between expressions, binteraction = -0.35, SE = 0.59, 95% CI [-1.50, 0.81], t(1122) = -0.59, p = .555.

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. stat_effect_size.title: Effect Sizes in t-tests and F-tests
stat_effect_size.summary_text: We found 17 t-tests and/or F-tests where effect sizes are not reported. Check these tests in the table below, and consider adding effect sizes.

table.text: As predicted, participants rated happy expressions as corresponding to more positive feelings than neutral expressions, intercept = 26.08, b = 54.90, SE = 1.11, 95% CI [52.71, 57.09], t(414) = 49.30, p < .001 (see Figure 1D).
table.d_coherence_note: No parseable d effect size found.

table.text: As predicted, participants were willing to pay more for tickets to lotteries associated with happy expressions than for lotteries associated with neutral expressions, intercept = 2.78, b = 3.41, SE = 0.10, 95% CI [3.22, 3.60], t(414) = 35.29, p < .001, corresponding to 34.1% of the response scale (see Figure 1E).
table.d_coherence_note: No parseable d effect size found.

table.text: Each additional rating point of inferred affect was associated with 0.045 pence higher WTP (i.e., about 0.45 pence per 10 points), b = 0.045, SE = 0.003, 95% CI [0.039, 0.051], t(749) = 14.24, p < .001.
table.d_coherence_note: No parseable d effect size found.

table.text: With inferred affect in the model, the effect of expression valence shrank from cE = 3.41 to c′E = 0.96, SE = 0.19, 95% CI [0.58, 1.34], t(681) = 4.95, p < .001.
table.d_coherence_note: No parseable d effect size found.

table.text: The relationship between inferred affect and WTP did not differ between neutral and happy expressions, binteraction = 0.0050, SE = 0.0063, 95% CI [-0.0074, 0.0175], t(614) = 0.79, p = .430.
table.d_coherence_note: No parseable d effect size found.

info.title: Group Membership Changes How Others' Affect Informs Observers' Valuation of Unseen Outcomes

author.affiliation:

text.text: Others' affective reactions can be the only available information about how good an outcome might be, yet little is known about how people use them to inform their own valuation.
Across three preregistered experiments, we tested how observers use others' reactions to value unseen lottery outcomes, and whether social group membership changes this affect-based value inference.

Participants observed facial reactions of "demonstrators" to hidden lottery outcomes, reported how good they believed the demonstrator felt about the outcome (inferred affect), and stated their incentive-compatible willingness to pay (WTP) for these lotteries.
In Experiment 1 (N = 416), happy relative to neutral expressions increased both inferred affect and WTP, and inferred affect accounted for most of the valuation difference.
Experiment 2 (N = 1,127; informed by piloting, N = 419) introduced group membership via political agreement.
In-group demonstrators were inferred to feel slightly better, and happy expressions increased WTP more when they came from in-group than from out-group demonstrators.
Experiment 3 (N = 1,461) replicated these findings and added angry expressions, which reduced WTP without significant group differences.
Across Experiments 2 and 3, group differences in reported inferred affect partially accounted for the group differences in valuation.
Our findings extend affect's role as a social signal to economic valuation and show that social group membership changes how others' reactions inform observers' valuation of unseen outcomes.
Affect may thus be one route by which preferences spread differently within identity-aligned groups.
Unseen Outcomes Imagine passing a restaurant you have never tried and catching the smile of someone leaving.
Their smile alone might leave you more inclined to try the restaurant yourself.

Others' affective reactions can be the only available source of information about the value of an outcome (e.g., food or reward), and yet relatively little is known about how people use others' affective reactions to inform their own valuation when no alternative source of information is available.
In parallel, people do not treat all social sources of information equally, frequently discriminating based on coalitions and group identities.
Imagine that the person leaving is someone you recognize as similar to you, or someone who clearly is not.
Would their perceived similarity or group membership change your valuation of their outcomes?

Here we induce these considerations to intersect, allowing us to ask both how others' affective expressions inform observers' subjective valuation of outcomes, and whether social group membership changes how these expressions inform valuation.

To address these questions, we combine approaches from affective science, social cognition, and behavioral economics to test whether observers use others' facial expressions to inform their subjective valuation.
We measure both how good observers think another person feels about their outcome (inferred affect) and how much observers are willing to pay for that outcome.

Inferred-affect ratings serve to approximate how observers interpret affective reactions, allowing us to probe associations between this form of social inference and observers' own valuation of outcomes.

A large body of work demonstrates that others' affective expressions serve as social signals that help observers to guide their own judgments and behavior (Hareli & Hess, 2012; Keltner et al., 2019; Keltner & Haidt, 1999; Van Kleef, 2009; Van Kleef & Côté, 2022).
text.formatted: A large body of work demonstrates that others' affective expressions serve as social signals that help observers to guide their own judgments and behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Hareli & Hess, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Keltner et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Keltner & Haidt, 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Van Kleef, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">Van Kleef & Côté, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Observers use others' emotional reactions to infer whether situations are cooperative or competitive (Van Doorn et al., 2012), whether norms have been violated (Hareli et al., 2013; Heerdink et al., 2019) and how to respond to unfamiliar objects or situations (Stenberg & Forslund, 2020; Walle et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Observers use others' emotional reactions to infer whether situations are cooperative or competitive <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">(Van Doorn et al., 2012)</ref>, whether norms have been violated <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Hareli et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Heerdink et al., 2019)</ref> and how to respond to unfamiliar objects or situations <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Stenberg & Forslund, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">Walle et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Infants use caregivers' expressions toward novel objects to decide whether to approach or avoid them (Klinnert et al., 1986).
text.formatted: Infants use caregivers' expressions toward novel objects to decide whether to approach or avoid them <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Klinnert et al., 1986)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, adults are more likely to avoid objects that they have previously observed paired with fearful rather than happy expressions (Meffert et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Similarly, adults are more likely to avoid objects that they have previously observed paired with fearful rather than happy expressions <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Meffert et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Together, this work establishes that affective expressions signal evaluative information that observers can use to guide their own behavior in novel contexts.
But do affective expressions also inform observers' formally measured valuation of unseen outcomes, beyond such measures of approach and avoidance?
Subjective value refers to how much an option is worth to an individual and is central to theories of learning and choice (Juechems & Summerfield, 2019; Rangel et al., 2008).
text.formatted: Subjective value refers to how much an option is worth to an individual and is central to theories of learning and choice <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Juechems & Summerfield, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Rangel et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: In reinforcement learning, subjective value (as estimated future reward) allows organisms to learn from experience and choose options that maximize expected reward (Juechems & Summerfield, 2019; Polanía et al., 2019; Rangel et al., 2008).
text.formatted: In reinforcement learning, subjective value (as estimated future reward) allows organisms to learn from experience and choose options that maximize expected reward <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Juechems & Summerfield, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Polanía et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Rangel et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: In the study of economic choice, subjective value (commonly measured via willingness to pay [WTP]; Becker et al., 1964) guides preferences between competing alternatives (Kable & Glimcher, 2007; Padoa-Schioppa & Assad, 2006; von Neumann et al., 1944).
text.formatted: In the study of economic choice, subjective value (commonly measured via willingness to pay <ref type="bibr">[WTP]</ref>; <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Becker et al., 1964)</ref> guides preferences between competing alternatives <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Kable & Glimcher, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Padoa-Schioppa & Assad, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">von Neumann et al., 1944)</ref>.

text.text: By focusing on subjective value measured as WTP, the present investigation extends beyond asking whether observed affect influences behavior and asks instead whether observed affect can serve as a signal that acts on the underlying valuation.
Why might another person's affective reaction provide information relevant to observers' own subjective valuation of an unseen outcome?
Work on experienced affect suggests that affective reactions compactly encode information relevant to valuation.
Positive outcomes generally elicit more positive affective reactions than negative outcomes (Forbes & Bennett, 2024; Mellers et al., 1999; Parr et al., 2026; Shenhav, 2024).
text.formatted: Positive outcomes generally elicit more positive affective reactions than negative outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Forbes & Bennett, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Mellers et al., 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Parr et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Shenhav, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, how good someone feels about an outcome (i.e., valence) tracks with how that outcome compares to their expectations (Chew et al., 2021; Rutledge et al., 2014), effectively approximating their subjective valuation of that reward (Vollberg & Sander, 2024).
text.formatted: Moreover, how good someone feels about an outcome (i.e., valence) tracks with how that outcome compares to their expectations <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Chew et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Rutledge et al., 2014)</ref>, effectively approximating their subjective valuation of that reward <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">(Vollberg & Sander, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Observed affect may therefore provide observers with usable information not only about an objective outcome value, but about how that value was subjectively experienced and evaluated by another person, or, in other words, information about objective outcomes through another person's subjective lens.
Whether observers rely on this information may well depend on the extent to which they expect the other person's preferences to align with their own.
Such expectations could be cued by shared group identity, which people can infer based on preference similarity in other domains (see next section ; Gershman & Cikara, 2020; Lau et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Such expectations could be cued by shared group identity, which people can infer based on preference similarity in other domains (see next section <ref type="bibr">;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Gershman & Cikara, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Lau et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Observers may also use others' affective reactions to infer value when the outcome that elicited the reactions is hidden.

To do so, observers may infer how the demonstrator feels about the experienced outcome (which people readily infer from facial information; Frank & Stennett, 2001; Klingner & Guntinas-Lichius, 2023; Lange et al., 2022), and draw on that inferred affective state when valuing the outcome for themselves.
text.formatted: To do so, observers may infer how the demonstrator feels about the experienced outcome (which people readily infer from facial information; <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Frank & Stennett, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Klingner & Guntinas-Lichius, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Lange et al., 2022)</ref>, and draw on that inferred affective state when valuing the outcome for themselves.

text.text: Put simply, an outcome that makes another person feel good may also be good for them.
We refer to the use of another person's affective reaction to infer the value of outcomes one has not personally experienced as affect-based value inference.

The first aim of the present work is to establish whether observers can use demonstrators' facial expressions to infer how good the demonstrator feels about a hidden outcome, in turn, adjust their own formally measured valuation of that outcome, and to probe how much of this valuation can be accounted for by inferred affect.

People categorize others into social groups with shared social identity based on shared preferences (Gershman & Cikara, 2020), including political opinions (Lau et al., 2018), and favor members of their own social group (in-group; Amodio & Cikara, 2021; Hewstone et al., 2002; Tajfel, 1970).
text.formatted: People categorize others into social groups with shared social identity based on shared preferences <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Gershman & Cikara, 2020)</ref>, including political opinions <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Lau et al., 2018)</ref>, and favor members of their own social group (in-group; <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Amodio & Cikara, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Hewstone et al., 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Tajfel, 1970)</ref>.

text.text: Such in-group favoritism also extends to learning.

Both adults (Boeltzig et al., 2023; Golkar et al., 2015; Golkar & Olsson, 2017; Kang et al., 2021) and children (Buttelmann et al., 2013; Howard et al., 2015) learn more readily from in-group than out-group members.
text.formatted: Both adults <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Boeltzig et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Golkar et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Golkar & Olsson, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Kang et al., 2021)</ref> and children <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Buttelmann et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Howard et al., 2015)</ref> learn more readily from in-group than out-group members.

text.text: For example, people observing the actions and outcomes of others in a reinforcement learning task learn less from individuals who oppose (i.e., outgroup) rather than share their political views (i.e., in-group members; Kang et al., 2021).
text.formatted: For example, people observing the actions and outcomes of others in a reinforcement learning task learn less from individuals who oppose (i.e., outgroup) rather than share their political views (i.e., in-group members; <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Kang et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, this deficit is explained by impaired learning from out-group actions, whereas learning from out-group outcomes remains intact, suggesting that group membership can selectively affect specific channels of social information when observers learn what value to expect from observing others.
Group membership can induce biases in domains unrelated to the content of the group identity and distort valuation and value updating.
People have been shown to learn from politically like-minded others, even when tasks are unrelated to politics (Marks et al., 2019).
text.formatted: People have been shown to learn from politically like-minded others, even when tasks are unrelated to politics <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Marks et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, social stereotypes distort valuation and value updating during repeated social interactions.

Even when objective rewards are equivalent across interaction partners, people favor positively over negatively stereotyped group members and incorporate positive feedback from negatively stereotyped group members less strongly into their preferences (Schultner, Lindström, et al., 2024; Schultner, Stillerman, et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Even when objective rewards are equivalent across interaction partners, people favor positively over negatively stereotyped group members and incorporate positive feedback from negatively stereotyped group members less strongly into their preferences <ref type="bibr">(Schultner, Lindström, et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Schultner, Stillerman, et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In other words, social group information can distort both what value observers expect from others and how new information updates those expectations.
Group membership may also change how rewarding others' outcomes are for observers.

Observing others receive rewards engages reward-related processing (Lockwood et al., 2015), and this signature of vicarious reward is more pronounced for others whom observers perceive as sharing their attitudes and values (Mobbs et al., 2009).
text.formatted: Observing others receive rewards engages reward-related processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Lockwood et al., 2015)</ref>, and this signature of vicarious reward is more pronounced for others whom observers perceive as sharing their attitudes and values <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Mobbs et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: These lines of work show that group membership can influence how people learn from and evaluate information provided by others.
Most of the previous work, however, has focused primarily on actions and outcomes as social information.
Here, we ask whether ingroup favoritism also manifests in value inferences from observing affective reactions of others, particularly to outcomes that are hidden.
This question is most relevant for situations in which affective expressions are observable but objective outcomes are not.
How could group membership influence affect-based value inference?
Two nonmutually exclusive possibilities follow from the reasoning above.
First, observers may infer different affect from the same expression and value the outcome accordingly.

Second, group membership may change how the inferred information informs observers' own valuation, for example because a positive reaction from someone who shares one's preferences says more about how much one would value the outcome oneself.
By measuring inferred affect, we can probe the first possibility directly and ask how much of the group effect on valuation (if any) can be accounted for by inferred affect.
A group effect on valuation that remains after accounting for inferred affect would point to the second possibility (without confirming it).

The second aim of the present work is therefore to test whether social group membership influences affect-based value inference and, if so, to describe how its effects on inferred affect and valuation are related.
Experiment 1 (N = 416) tested whether observers can use others' affective reactions to hidden outcomes to inform their subjective valuation of those outcomes.

Participants observed a demonstrator reacting to two hidden lottery outcomes with either a neutral or happy facial expression (Ma et al., 2015), reported how positively they inferred the demonstrator to have felt about the outcome, and reported their WTP for a ticket to the lottery using an incentive-compatible Becker-DeGroot-Marschak procedure (BDM; Becker et al., 1964).
text.formatted: Participants observed a demonstrator reacting to two hidden lottery outcomes with either a neutral or happy facial expression <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Ma et al., 2015)</ref>, reported how positively they inferred the demonstrator to have felt about the outcome, and reported their WTP for a ticket to the lottery using an incentive-compatible Becker-DeGroot-Marschak procedure (BDM; <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Becker et al., 1964)</ref>.

text.text: We hypothesized that happy (vs. neutral) expressions would lead observers to infer more positive affect (H1) and higher WTP (H2), and probed how much of the effect of expression on WTP could be accounted for by inferred affect.
Experiment 2 (N = 1,127) built on extensive piloting (N = 419; see Supplementary Materials) to examine whether and how affect-based value inference is influenced by social group membership.

Participants observed both an in-group and out-group demonstrator, operationalized via political agreement (Gershman & Cikara, 2020; Kang et al., 2021), reacting to two hidden lottery outcomes each with a neutral and a happy expression.
text.formatted: Participants observed both an in-group and out-group demonstrator, operationalized via political agreement <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Gershman & Cikara, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Kang et al., 2021)</ref>, reacting to two hidden lottery outcomes each with a neutral and a happy expression.

text.text: We hypothesized that in-group demonstrators would be inferred to feel more positive than outgroup demonstrators at the same expression level (H3), and that happy expressions would increase WTP more when coming from in-group compared to out-group demonstrators (H4).
We further examined how much of the in-group effect on WTP could be accounted for by the in-group effect on inferred affect.

Experiment 3 (N = 1,461) extended the previous experiments by testing how people use negative reactions (i.e., anger) to inform their subjective valuation of unseen outcomes, and whether social group membership influences affect-based value inferences from such negative expressions.
Each participant observed two in-group and two out-group demonstrators reacting with neutral, happy, and angry expressions.
We tested whether Experiment 2's findings replicated in this setting and whether group membership also changed the effect of angry expressions on WTP.

Experiment 1 tested whether observers can use demonstrators' facial expressions to infer how positively the demonstrator feels about a hidden lottery outcome, and whether these expressions and inferences about them influence the observer's own subjective valuation for a ticket to that lottery measured via WTP (Becker et al., 1964).
text.formatted: Experiment 1 tested whether observers can use demonstrators' facial expressions to infer how positively the demonstrator feels about a hidden lottery outcome, and whether these expressions and inferences about them influence the observer's own subjective valuation for a ticket to that lottery measured via WTP <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Becker et al., 1964)</ref>.

text.text: Each participant observed one demonstrator reacting to two lottery outcomes with either a neutral or happy facial expression.
We recruited 420 participants via Prolific.
Participants' first language had to be English and their current country of residence had to be the United States.
Participants were compensated at a base rate of £9 per hour and earned an additional bonus based on their WTP responses (see Design and Procedure).

Participants who did not provide informed consent or failed the attention check were excluded (n = 4), resulting in a final sample of N = 416 participants (n = 217 female, n = 197 male, n = 2 other; age: M = 42.62, SD = 14.20, range = 18-80).
Data were collected on March 18, 2026.
The design, hypotheses, and analysis plan were preregistered prior to data collection.
Sample size was determined a priori via Monte Carlo power simulation targeting H2 (the effect of expression valence on WTP).

Because no prior estimate was available, simulations were based on synthetic data with a smallest effect of interest of 0.5 pence (WTP difference between happy and neutral expressions), and we targeted the conventional 80% power.
The simulation model included random intercepts for participant and demonstrator, as preregistered (see Supplementary Materials for details).
With 1,000 iterations per candidate sample size, simulations indicated that N = 400 participants would yield approximately 80% power to detect this effect at α = .05.
We recruited 420 participants to account for potential exclusions.
Demonstrator faces were selected from the Chicago Face Database (CFD; Ma et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Demonstrator faces were selected from the Chicago Face Database (CFD; <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Ma et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: To be suitable for the experimental design, models were required to have a neutral, a happy closed-mouth, and (for Experiment 3) an angry expression available, which restricted the selection pool to Black Female, Black Male, White Female and White Male models.

We used a three-stage selection procedure to select three models from each of these four groups: First, eligibility filtering retained only models with the requisite expression sets and unambiguous gender and ethnicity classifications, operationalized as classification probabilities of at least .95 on the relevant CFD norming variables (FemaleProb or MaleProb ≥ .95; BlackProb or WhiteProb ≥ .95).
Second, based on the CFD norming data, models rated more than 0.5 SD above their group mean on "unusualness" and 0.5 SD below their group mean on "prototypicality" were excluded.

Third, the remaining models were matched across groups on thirteen CFD norming dimensions: perceived age, attractiveness, trustworthiness, dominance, threat, babyfacedness, suitability as a research stimulus, and the perceived intensity of six emotions on the neutral face (happy, sad, angry, afraid, disgusted, surprised).
Each variable was z-scored across the full filtered dataset, and the Euclidean distance from each model to the cross-group centroid was computed.
Within each group, models were ranked by their distance to this common centroid (Supplementary Materials Table S4).
text.formatted: Within each group, models were ranked by their distance to this common centroid (Supplementary Materials Table <ref type="table">S4</ref>).

text.text: In Experiment 1, the closest model of each group served as the demonstrator for the main trials and the neutral expression of the second-closest model as the example-trial stimulus.
Each participant observed a single demonstrator displaying both a neutral and a happy closed-mouth expression across two total trials (within-participants manipulation of expression valence).
On each trial, participants rated how good they thought the demonstrator felt about a lottery outcome and how much they would be willing to pay for a ticket to that lottery.
WTP responses were incentivized using a BDM procedure (Becker et al., 1964) to ensure participants reported their true valuation of the ticket.
text.formatted: WTP responses were incentivized using a BDM procedure <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Becker et al., 1964)</ref> to ensure participants reported their true valuation of the ticket.

text.text: After providing informed consent and completing a general attention-check item ("How many times have you personally visited the planet Mars?"
; single-choice options 0-9), participants were introduced to the main task.

Participants were told that they would observe a person reacting to outcomes from different lotteries paying between 1 and 10 pence (i.e., £0.01 to £0.10), with some lotteries paying more than others.
The instructions read: "In each round, you will see the person's facial reaction to their lottery outcome.
Your task is to use this information to evaluate the lottery for yourself."
No other information about the demonstrator or the purpose of their reaction was provided.

Based on this information, participants were instructed to provide two ratings on each trial: a) how good they believe the person feels about their outcome (inferred affect), and b) how much they would be willing to pay for a ticket to that lottery (WTP).
The BDM procedure was then explained: At the end of the experiment, one trial would be randomly selected and a random ticket price between 1 and 10 pence would be drawn.

If the participant's WTP for that trial met or exceeded the drawn price, the participant would pay the drawn price from their 10 pence budget and receive the lottery's payout and their remaining budget as a bonus.
If the participant's WTP was below the drawn price, no transaction would occur and they would receive their bidding budget of 10 pence as a bonus.
Participants then completed an example trial followed by comprehension check questions, which had to be repeated until answered correctly before the main task began.

Each participant was randomly assigned to view a demonstrator from one of the four demonstrator groups described above, and the order in which the two expressions were presented was randomized across participants.

Inferred affect thus accounted for most of the expression effect on WTP, consistent with the idea that observers value an outcome to a substantial degree according to how good they infer the demonstrator to feel about it.

Experiment 1 showed that observers used demonstrators' facial expressions to infer how good the demonstrator felt about a hidden outcome and adjusted their incentivecompatible valuation of that outcome accordingly, with inferred affect accounting for most of this effect (72%).
We treat inferred affect-observers' reported inference about how good the demonstrator feels about the outcome-as a proxy for their interpretation of the demonstrator's affective response.
However, that does not mean that inferred affect captures all the information observers extract from an expression.
Observers may, for instance, also form inferences about the demonstrator (Dashti et al., 2026) or about how valuable the outcome was for the demonstrator.
text.formatted: Observers may, for instance, also form inferences about the demonstrator <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Dashti et al., 2026)</ref> or about how valuable the outcome was for the demonstrator.

text.text: The latter inferences about value inherently overlap with inferred affect to the extent that affective valence reflects subjective value (Shenhav, 2024; Vollberg & Sander, 2024).
text.formatted: The latter inferences about value inherently overlap with inferred affect to the extent that affective valence reflects subjective value <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Shenhav, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Vollberg & Sander, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, a single rating measures the inference with noise, and WTP may not change linearly with inferred affect.
It is therefore not surprising that inferred affect did not account for the entire expression effect.
That said, our results show that a single proxy of how good observers interpreted the demonstrator to feel predicted how they valued the outcome themselves, even beyond the expression category.
In Experiment 1, the demonstrators were anonymous strangers with no further information provided about them.
Often, however, we know more about the people whose reactions we observe, such as whether they share our views or not.
Experiment 2 therefore asked whether value inference from affective reactions changes with political similarity between participants and demonstrators.
Happy Facial Expressions Experiment 2 introduced political group-related information by telling participants whether the observed demonstrators shared their views.
Before observing each demonstrator, participants learned whether the demonstrator agreed with most or with few of their own political opinions.

Following prior work that used shared preferences and political agreement to induce group membership (Gershman & Cikara, 2020; Kang et al., 2021; Lau et al., 2018), we refer to demonstrators who largely agreed with the participant as in-group and to those who largely disagreed as out-group demonstrators.

We recruited 1,168 participants via Prolific (same participation requirements and compensation as in Experiment 1).

Participants who failed either of two attention checks were excluded (n = 41), resulting in a final sample of N = 1,127 participants (n = 602 female, n = 517 male, n = 8 other; age: M = 39.68, SD = 12.77, range = 18-81).
Data were collected on April 23, 2026.
The design, hypotheses, and analysis plan were preregistered prior to data collection.

Sample size was determined a priori via Monte Carlo power simulation (1,000 iterations per candidate sample size) for the H4 interaction (expression valence × group membership on WTP), based on a pilot study with the same design (N = 419; see Supplementary Materials).
The target effect was the pilot estimate of this interaction (b = 0.29 pence).
We targeted 90% rather than 80% power to buffer against imprecise pilot estimates.
Simulations indicated that N = 1,060 participants would yield approximately 90% power to detect this effect at α = .05.
We planned to recruit 1,166 participants to account for potential exclusions; due to minor over-recruitment on Prolific, 1,168 participants took part.

Each demonstrator was then presented with a profile of responses that randomly matched either four out of five of the participant's responses (ingroup) or only one out of five (out-group) at the beginning of their lottery trials.

The design and procedure was similar to Experiment 1 with the addition of the following changes: The expression-valence manipulation was crossed with a withinparticipant manipulation of demonstrator group membership, yielding a 2 (expression valence: neutral vs. happy) × 2 (group membership: out-group vs. in-group) fully withinparticipant design with four trials per participant.
Before the lottery task instructions, participants reported their own positions on the five political-opinion items.
Each participant observed two demonstrators in total.
Both demonstrators were drawn from the same CFD model group (Black Female, Black Male, White Female, or White Male), randomly assigned across participants and held constant within participants.

The two closest models of the selected group (see Stimulus Selection in Experiment 1) were randomly assigned to the in-group and the out-group role, and the neutral expression of the third-closest model was shown in the example trial.

At the start of each demonstrator block, participants were shown the demonstrator's responses to the five political-opinion items sequentially, establishing them as either an in-group (4/5 agreement) or out-group (1/5 agreement) member.
The order of demonstrator blocks (in-group first vs. out-group first) was randomized across participants, as was the order of expression valence (neutral first vs. happy first) within each block.
Parallel to Experiment 1, at the end of each demonstrator block, participants indicated which of the two lotteries they believed had paid more for that demonstrator.

After completing both demonstrator blocks, participants rated their social affinity toward each demonstrator, that is, how much they liked, valued, and felt connected to them (separate scales from0 = not at all to100 = very much), presented in the order in which the demonstrators had appeared during the experiment.

Moreover, after providing demographic information and responding to open questions about their experience in the study, participants completed a post-study attention check indicating which model group the presented demonstrators belonged to, with response options covering the four possible groups (Black Female, Black Male, White Female, White Male).
The trial structure, rating scales and BDM incentivization were otherwise identical to Experiment 1.
Median completion time was 13.5 minutes.

Three secondary tests were no longer significant (in Experiment 2, the weighting term and the happy-neutral difference in path b; in Experiment 3, the happy vs. angry difference in the indirect effect).
As preregistered, path estimates are reported without adjustment for multiple comparisons.
Expression valence and group membership were manipulated within participants, so their effects on inferred affect and WTP (H1-H4) are experimental effects.

Inferred affect, in contrast, was measured, so the path analyses describe how the experimental in-group effects on inferred affect and WTP are related and do not identify causal mediation (see Experiment 1).
The analyses are nonetheless informative because they constrain explanations of the in-group effects.

Specifically, if the in-group effect on WTP rested only on in-group demonstrators being inferred to feel better, inferred affect should account for it, provided that WTP changes linearly with inferred affect (non-linear mappings are tested in Experiment 3).

In-group demonstrators were inferred to feel slightly better (H3), and happy expressions increased WTP more when they came from in-group demonstrators (H4).
One explanation for these results could be that observers valued in-group reactions more because they inferred in-group demonstrators to feel better.
This explanation predicts that inferred affect accounts for the in-group effect on WTP (see Analysis).
If it does not, explanations must go beyond how good observers inferred the demonstrator to feel.

To examine this, we estimated the paths shown in Figure 4, corresponding to the following questions: Is increased WTP for in-group members accompanied by more positive inferred affect (indirect effect via inferred affect, aG × b)?

Across expressions, in-group demonstrators were inferred to feel 1.07 rating points better than outgroup demonstrators (p = .001; Figure 3C), and this difference did not differ between expressions (difference = -0.35, t(1122) = -0.59, p = .555; neutral: aG = 1.24; happy: aG = 0.89; full statistics under H3).

text.text: Path b asks whether observers were willing to pay more when they inferred the demonstrator to feel better.
We added inferred affect to the additive WTP model:

Because expression valence and group membership are also in the model, b compares trials with the same expression and the same group membership that differ in how good the demonstrator was inferred to feel; it does not repeat the large difference in inferred affect between happy and neutral expressions.
Inferred affect is entered in raw rating points (rescaled for fitting as in Experiment 1), so b is the change in WTP (in pence) per rating point.

Across expressions, each additional rating point was associated with 0.049 pence higher WTP (about 0.5 pence per 10 points), b = 0.049, SE = 0.002, 95% CI [0.046, 0.053], t(918) = 31.33, p < .001 (Figure 3D).

text.text: To test whether b differed between expressions, and to estimate the direct effect for each expression (see below), we used a model in which each expression had its own slope of inferred affect and its own in-group effect:

In this model, the expression valence × inferred affect term tests whether b differs between expressions, and the expression valence × group membership term allows the ingroup effect on WTP to differ between expressions, as H4 showed it does.
The slope was slightly steeper for happy (b = 0.053) than for neutral expressions (b = 0.048; difference = 0.0051, SE = 0.0025, 95% CI [0.0001, 0.0100], t(1570) = 2.01, p = .045).
This difference was not significant under the common random-effects structure (p = .061; Table S12).

text.text: The indirect effect aG × b is the in-group difference in WTP that would be implied by the in-group difference in inferred affect and the slope b.
As in Experiment 1, we tested this indirect effect with a Monte Carlo 95% CI.

Across expressions (aG from the additive H3 model, b from the additive model above), the indirect effect was 0.053 pence, 95% CI [0.021, 0.085], corresponding to 34% of the total in-group effect on WTP (cG = 0.15 pence, p < .001; additive H4 model; Figure 3F).
text.formatted: Across expressions (aG from the additive H3 model, b from the additive model above), the indirect effect was 0.053 pence, 95% CI [0.021, 0.085], corresponding to 34% of the total in-group effect on WTP (cG = 0.15 pence, p < .001; additive H4 model; Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">3F</ref>).

text.text: The indirect effect did not differ between expressions (difference = -0.012 pence, 95% CI [-0.070, 0.046]; neutral: 0.059 pence, 95% CI [0.018, 0.101]; happy: 0.047 pence, 95% CI [0.002, 0.093]).
For neutral expressions, the indirect effect was thus significantly positive, although the total in-group effect on WTP was not significant (cG = 0.05, p = .264).
A nonsignificant total effect does not show that the total effect is zero, and the total effect approximately equals the sum of the indirect and the direct effect (here,0.05 ≈ 0.06 + 0.00 pence).
Moreover, the two effects are estimated with different precision, so that an indirect effect can be detected when a total effect is not (Rucker et al., 2011).

text.text: For neutral expressions, the slightly more positive inferred affect of ingroup demonstrators thus corresponded to a WTP difference too small to be detected as a total effect.

The direct effect c′G is the in-group effect on WTP in the models with inferred affect, that is, the difference in WTP between an in-group and an out-group demonstrator who showed the same expression and were inferred to feel equally good (conditional association).
Across expressions, WTP was higher after in-group reactions at equal inferred affect, c′G = 0.11, SE = 0.03, 95% CI [0.06, 0.16], t(1092) = 3.99, p < .001 (Figure 3G).

text.text: The direct effect differed between expressions (difference = 0.21, SE = 0.05, 95% CI [0.11, 0.31], t(1102) = 4.17, p < .001), and was significant for happy expressions, c′G = 0.22, SE = 0.04, 95% CI [0.14, 0.29], t(2175) = 5.76, p < .001, but not for neutral expressions, c′G = 0.00, SE = 0.04, 95% CI [-0.07, 0.08], t(2204) = 0.09, p = .928.

text.text: Thus, the direct in-group effect across expressions appears to be carried by happy expressions.
Finally, as a follow-up, we asked whether the same increase in inferred affect was associated with a larger increase in WTP for in-group than for out-group demonstrators showing the same expression.
To test this, we added a group membership × inferred affect interaction term to the model with expression-specific slopes:
Here, the weighting term wG is the coefficient of the group membership × inferred affect interaction, that is, the difference between the in-group and the out-group slope of inferred affect.

Because the model also contains expression valence × group membership and expression valence × inferred affect, wG compares in-group and out-group slopes within the same expression, after allowing each expression its own in-group effect on WTP and its own slope of inferred affect.
In this model, wG takes one value for both expressions.

Inferred affect was slightly more strongly associated with WTP for in-group demonstrators, wG = 0.0035, SE = 0.0016, 95% CI [0.0004, 0.0067], t(2364) = 2.18, p = .030 (pence per rating point; Figure 3H).

text.text: To test whether the weighting differed between expressions, we added the three-way interaction term (expression valence × group membership × inferred affect), which allows separate wG for each expression.

The weighting did not differ between expressions (difference = 0.0004, t(2404) = 0.11, p = .915) and was not significant for either expression on its own (neutral: wG = 0.0034, 95% CI [-0.0004, 0.0073], p = .083; happy: wG = 0.0038, 95% CI [-0.0018, 0.0093], p = .183; Table S12).

text.text: Notably, weighting could also be tested without the expression valence × group membership term, but that would address a different question.

Specifically, because happy expressions are inferred to be more positive than neutral ones, a steeper in-group slope of inferred affect in such a model would merely capture the interaction tested under H4 (see Supplementary Materials, Table S14).

text.text: Including the additional term, however, allows us to ask whether inferred affect is more strongly associated with WTP for in-group demonstrators beyond expression effects already established under H4.
As in Experiment 1, we finally asked how much of the effect of expression valence on WTP was accounted for by inferred affect.

Across in-group and out-group demonstrators, aE was the expression effect on inferred affect (additive H3 model), the total effect cE the expression effect on WTP (additive H4 model), and b and the direct effect c′E came from the additive model with inferred affect above.
A single direct expression effect requires one slope of inferred affect for both expressions, so the model with expressionspecific slopes was not used here.
As in Experiment 1, inferred affect accounted for most of the expression effect on WTP.
The indirect effect was 2.67 pence, 95% CI [2.45, 2.89], or 84% of the total effect (cE = 3.19), with a remaining direct effect of c′E = 0.56, SE = 0.08, 95% CI [0.41, 0.72], t(600) = 7.19, p < .001.

text.text: In Experiment 2, whether demonstrators shared participants' political opinions (ingroup) or opposed them (out-group) changed affect-based value inference.

Observers inferred in-group demonstrators to feel slightly better (H3), and happy expressions increased WTP more when they came from in-group demonstrators (H4), while the effects of expression valence on inferred affect and WTP replicated Experiment 1.
The more positive inferred affect ratings for in-group demonstrators accounted for part of the in-group effect on WTP.
The remaining in-group effect has at least two interpretations.
In-group reactions may inform valuation differently (e.g., a premium for positive in-group signals), or the inferred-affect rating may not capture everything observers infer from a reaction.
Experiment 2 thus shows that in-group reactions raised WTP beyond what inferred affect could account for, and this in-group effect was larger for happy than for neutral expressions.

Experiment 2 included only neutral and happy expressions, which leaves room to ask how observers use negative reactions to value unseen outcomes and whether group membership also changes valuation from such reactions.

Moreover, it remained untested whether participants perceived agreeing demonstrators as closer to their own political party (as a conceptualization of a social in-group) and disagreeing demonstrators as members of the other party (out-group), rather than only as sharing or not sharing their opinions.
Angry Expressions To address these questions, we conducted a third experiment that included angry expressions.

This allowed us to test how observers use negative reactions to value unseen outcomes, whether group membership also changes this valuation, and whether the results of Experiment 2 hold when negative reactions are part of the stimulus set.

For every demonstrator, and before any expression was shown, participants also indicated which political party they believed the demonstrator felt closer to, and at the end of the study they rated the two parties, testing whether the agreement manipulation induced perceived political group membership.

Finally, to increase the precision of within-participant estimates at an adequate study length, each participant completed twelve rather than four trials (four demonstrators with three expressions each).
We recruited 1,508 participants via Prolific (same participation requirements as in Experiments 1 and 2).

Participants who failed any of three attention checks were excluded (n = 47), resulting in a final sample of N = 1,461 participants (n = 790 female, n = 656 male, n = 15 other; age: M = 41.53, SD = 13.12, range = 18-88).
Data were collected on October 2, 2026.
The design, hypotheses, and analysis plan were preregistered prior to data collection.

Sample size was determined a priori by simulation (1,000 simulations per specification) for the expression valence [happy] × group membership [in-group] interaction on WTP (H4), using variance components from a pilot sample (N = 97 after exclusions).

(2014), namely the lower bound of the 60% confidence interval of the Experiment 2 estimate under its preregistered random-effects structure (b = 0.23 pence, SE = 0.09), rescaled to the payout range of Experiment 3 (b = 0.19 pence).

text.text: We planned to recruit 1,490 participants to account for an expected exclusion rate of 6%; due to minor over-recruitment on Prolific, 1,508 participants took part.
Group membership was manipulated as in Experiment 2, with the following changes.
First, each participant observed two in-group and two out-group demonstrators (four demonstrators in total).

One in-group demonstrator agreed with all five and the other with four of the participant's five responses, and one out-group demonstrator agreed with one and the other with none of the participant's responses (agreement levels and agreeing items were randomly assigned).
Second, the demonstrator's responses were shown all at once next to the participant's own responses, followed by the number of shared opinions.

Third, after answering the opinion items, participants indicated which of the two major U.S. parties they felt closer to, and by how much, on a slider from "much closer to the Democratic Party" through "equally close to both parties" to "much closer to the Republican Party" (internally coded from -100 to +100 for analysis; a live readout showed the direction and strength unsigned, e.g., "Leaning Democratic 45").
After each demonstrator's opinion profile, and before any of the demonstrator's expressions, participants used the same slider to indicate which party they thought the demonstrator felt closer to.
This perceived placement served as the main manipulation check.

At the end of the study, participants rated how much they liked, valued, felt connected to, and trusted Democrats and Republicans in general (0-100) and, as in Experiment 2, reported their party identification (Democrat, Republican, or neither).
The design and procedure was similar to Experiment 2 but introduced several changes.
Expression valence had three levels (neutral, happy, and angry), yielding a 3 (expression valence) × 2 (group membership) fully within-participant design with twelve trials per participant.
Each participant observed four demonstrators.
Two of the four demonstrator groups (Black female, Black male, White female, White male) were randomly drawn for each participant.

The two models of each drawn group (the same eight models as in Experiment 2) were randomly assigned to the in-group and the out-group role, so that each participant saw one in-group and one out-group with the same race and gender.
The example trial showed the neutral expression of one of these eight models from a group not otherwise shown to the participant.
Demonstrators were introduced by first names that were randomly assigned within gender (Danielle, Stephanie, Nicole, Gabrielle; Kevin, Travis, Aaron, Derek).
text.formatted: Demonstrators were introduced by first names that were randomly assigned within gender <ref type="bibr">(Danielle, Stephanie, Nicole, Gabrielle; Kevin, Travis, Aaron, Derek)</ref>.

text.text: Names were chosen to be common and to fit Black and White demonstrators about equally well (Supplementary Materials, S5).
The order of demonstrators and the order of expressions within each demonstrator block were randomized.
Lotteries paid between 3 and 15 pence, and each trial showed a new lottery labeled by a random three-digit number.
Inferred affect was rated on a slider from -100 (very bad) through 0 (neutral) to +100 (very good), and WTP was entered as a whole number between 0 and 15 pence.
The BDM procedure could draw ticket prices between 1 and 15 pence.

After the second and fourth demonstrator blocks, participants completed an attention check indicating which group the demonstrator they had just observed belonged to (Black Female, Black Male, White Female, White Male).
Unlike in Experiments 1 and 2, participants were not asked which lottery had paid more.
Median completion time was 16.1 minutes.

text.text: Analyses followed the same approach as in Experiments 1 and 2, with neutral expressions and out-group demonstrators as reference levels.
As preregistered, we tested whether participants perceived agreeing demonstrators as members of their own political party (preregistered manipulation check).
To this end, we recoded each demonstrator's perceived placement so that positive values indicate the participant's own side.

If the agreement manipulation induced perceived political group membership as intended, demonstrators with high opinion overlap (i.e., in-group) should be placed noticeably closer on the participant's own side than out-group demonstrators.

The own side was defined either by participants' own slider placement (excluding participants at 0) or by their party identification in the demographics section of the study (excluding participants who identified with neither party), and perceived placement was regressed on group membership:

To test whether participants also felt more favorably toward their own party in general, ratings of the own and the other party were compared for each item and their mean, using the same two definitions of the own party:

Finally, as in Experiment 2, we tested whether the opinion items reflected partisan identity by regressing the number of left-leaning opinion responses (0-5) on participants' own placement and, separately, on party identification (Democrat vs.
Republican).

Besides replicating the happy vs. neutral findings of Experiments 1 and 2, we expected participants to infer more negative affect for angry than for neutral expressions and to be willing to pay less for the corresponding lotteries.

H1 and H2 were tested with the same random-effects structure as in Experiment 2, that is, with random intercepts for participants, demonstrators, and their pairs and random slopes of expression valence for participants and demonstrators.
H3 and H4 were tested with additive and interactive models.
Compared with Experiment 2, the selected structure additionally included random slopes of group membership for participants, so that the in-group effect could vary between participants:

As preregistered, H3 asked whether in-group demonstrators are rated as feeling better (additive model) and whether this depends on the expression (interactive model); H4 asked whether the happy × in-group interaction on WTP replicates and whether group membership also changes the effect of angry expressions.
In-group effects within each expression were estimated as in Experiment 2.

We related the in-group effects on inferred affect and WTP with the same models as in Experiment 2 (indirect effect, direct effect, and weighting, as well as the expression effects via inferred affect), now comparing the three expressions pairwise (happy vs. neutral, angry vs. neutral, happy vs. angry).
As in Experiment 2, the preregistered per-expression path models are reported in the Supplementary Materials (Table S11).

text.text: This follows from using one slope of inferred affect for all expressions in this analysis (b = 0.028).

Applied to the much lower inferred affect of angry expressions, this common slope predicts a larger drop in WTP than observed, because the slope for angry expressions was in fact shallower (b = 0.021; see above), and the positive direct effect absorbs the difference.
One possible contributor is that the lotteries paid at least 3 pence in our design, and mean WTP after angry expressions (about 3 pence) was close to this minimum.
In other words, angry expressions lowered WTP less than their lower inferred affect would imply under a single slope for all expressions.
Experiment 3 replicated both in-group effects of Experiment 2 with twelve trials per participant and additionally introduced angry faces.
In-group demonstrators were inferred to feel slightly better, and happy expressions increased WTP more when they came from ingroup demonstrators.

Angry expressions lowered WTP without a significant group difference, possibly because WTP after angry expressions was close to the minimum payout of 3 pence, leaving little room for group differences.
Unlike in Experiment 2, WTP was also higher for in-group demonstrators showing neutral expressions, possibly because neutral expressions were no longer the most negative reaction.
Inferred affect accounted for part (i.e., 19%) of the in-group effect on WTP.

Most of the in-group valuation premium remained when accounting for inferred affect, and this premium corresponded to the positivity of the expression, that is, largest for happy, smaller for neutral, and not detectable for angry expressions.
Non-linear mappings yielded the same premium, and group differences in the association between inferred affect and WTP within expressions were not significant.

Together with Experiment 2, these results show that in-group reactions increased valuation beyond what could be accounted for by the intergroup difference in inferred affect, and that this in-group effect is larger the more positive the reaction.

Across three preregistered experiments, we tested whether observers use others' affective reactions to inform their own valuation of outcomes they have not experienced themselves, and whether social group membership, induced via political agreement, alters affect-based value inference.

Experiment 1 established that observers inferred happy facial expressions to reflect more positive affect than neutral expressions and were willing to pay more for lotteries associated with them, with inferred affect accounting for most of this expression effect.
Experiments 2 and 3 showed that demonstrator group membership, induced via political agreement and perceived as shared partisan identity (Experiment 3), influences both affect ratings and WTP.

In-group demonstrators were inferred to feel slightly better, and happy expressions increased WTP more when they came from in-group demonstrators, whereas group membership did not significantly change the effect of angry expressions.
One explanation would be that observers valued in-group reactions more because they interpreted them as happier.
Relating the in-group effects on inferred affect and WTP showed this explanation to be at least incomplete.
While more positive inferred affect did account for part of the in-group effect on WTP, most of the in-group effect remained, especially for happy expressions.
We did not observe reliable group differences in how strongly inferred affect was associated with WTP within expressions.

In short, observers can use others' facial reactions to value outcomes they cannot see, while placing a valuation premium on positive reactions from political allies, which cannot be fully explained by how good they infer those allies to feel.

Together, these findings extend the study of affective signaling to subjective value as measured in behavioral economics and show that the group membership of the person whose reaction observers see changes how that reaction informs their valuation of unseen outcomes.

A large body of work has established that others' affective expressions serve as social signals that observers use to infer situational features and norms and to guide their own behavior in novel contexts (Hareli & Hess, 2012; Stenberg & Forslund, 2020; Van Kleef, 2009; Van Kleef & Côté, 2022; Walle et al., 2017).

text.text: Observers inferred happy expressions to reflect more positive affect about an outcome and were willing to pay more for tickets to lotteries associated with happy reactions.

Moreover, in all three experiments, a substantial part of the link between others' affective expressions and observers' WTP could be accounted for by how good observers inferred the demonstrator to feel.
This pattern is consistent with observers using others' affective reactions as a cue to what an outcome is worth and updating their own valuation accordingly.

Our findings operationalize, at the interpersonal level, the proposal that affective valence indexes or even constitutes subjective value (Shenhav, 2024; Vollberg et al., 2025; Vollberg & Sander, 2024).
text.formatted: Our findings operationalize, at the interpersonal level, the proposal that affective valence indexes or even constitutes subjective value <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Shenhav, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">Vollberg et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Vollberg & Sander, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Where prior work has shown that people's own affective reactions track with their subjective valuation of outcomes they experience (Chew et al., 2021; Forbes & Bennett, 2024; Mellers et al., 1999; Parr et al., 2026; Rutledge et al., 2014; Vanhasbroeck et al., 2021), the present results suggest that observers can use another person's affect as a window into how that person evaluated an outcome (Vollberg & Sander, 2024), and use this window to inform their own valuation.
