text.text: Because WTP was combined with an incentive-compatible BDM procedure, these shifts reflect valuation with monetary consequences.

In doing so, the present findings extend beyond observed affect as a signal that influences approach and avoidance (Klinnert et al., 1986; Meffert et al., 2015) and demonstrate that it acts on the valuation that ultimately determines choice.
text.formatted: In doing so, the present findings extend beyond observed affect as a signal that influences approach and avoidance <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Klinnert et al., 1986;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Meffert et al., 2015)</ref> and demonstrate that it acts on the valuation that ultimately determines choice.

text.text: Across Experiments 2 and 3, observers inferred demonstrators who shared their political opinions to feel slightly better than demonstrators who opposed them, despite seeing the same expressions.
Experiment 3 helps to interpret this shift.
If in-group expressions were simply interpreted as more typical of the displayed emotion, in-group angry expressions should have been interpreted as expressing more negative valence.
Instead, in-group angry expressions were interpreted as slightly less negative and in-group happy expressions as slightly more positive than the same expressions from out-group demonstrators.
This pattern is consistent with a shift toward more positive inferred affect for in-group demonstrators.
Whether it reflects more positive interpretations of in-group expressions, more negative interpretations of out-group expressions, or both, cannot be determined without an unaffiliated comparison.
These results complement prior work on observational learning and group bias (Boeltzig et al., 2023; Kang et al., 2021; Schultner, Lindström, et al., 2024; Schultner, Stillerman, et al., 2024).
text.formatted: These results complement prior work on observational learning and group bias <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Boeltzig et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Kang et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Schultner, Lindström, et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Schultner, Stillerman, et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: When rewards are hidden, observers can infer others' success from their observable behavior and selectively learn from those they infer to be successful (Hawkins et al., 2023).
text.formatted: When rewards are hidden, observers can infer others' success from their observable behavior and selectively learn from those they infer to be successful <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Hawkins et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The present work shows that others' affective reactions can serve a similar function for valuation, and that group identity (here induced via political agreement) can influence valuation even when neither actions nor outcomes are available, leaving affective reactions as the only information available.

In cases where outcomes are private (i.e., not yet experienced by observers) but reactions are public, positive reactions may therefore act more strongly on observers' valuation when they come from an identityaligned group than when they cross group lines.
This points to affect as one route by which preferences for outcomes (e.g., products or causes) may spread differently within identityaligned social groups.
We note that in-group effects were small relative to the effects of expressions themselves.

However, consistent across experiments, observers were willing to pay about 4.5% more after happy reactions from in-group demonstrators relative to what they were willing to pay after happy reactions from out-group demonstrators.
Such small effects can nevertheless have large consequences when they accumulate over many instances (Carey et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Such small effects can nevertheless have large consequences when they accumulate over many instances <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Carey et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: When populations are divided and people see others' reactions frequently, a consistent premium for positive reactions from like-minded others could add up and reinforce the alignment of preferences within groups.
Relating the in-group effects on inferred affect and WTP constrains possible explanations for the in-group effect on valuation.

Group membership influenced observers' reported inferences about the demonstrators' affective states, but the corresponding differences in inferred affect accounted for only part of the in-group effect on WTP.
Explanations that rest solely on in-group demonstrators being inferred to be happier are thus insufficient.

The remaining in-group valuation premium, largest for happy and absent for angry expressions, could reflect (i) systematic differences in how inferred affect informs valuation, (ii) additional evaluative inferences not captured by the inferred-affect rating, or both.
The first possibility, namely that inferred affect informs valuation differently for ingroup demonstrators, ties back to the reasoning that motivated this work.

Observers may assume in-group members to share their preferences (particularly given political agreement; Gershman & Cikara, 2020; Lau et al., 2018) and extend this assumption to economic preferences (much as people prefer to learn from politically like-minded others even on nonpolitical tasks; Marks et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Observers may assume in-group members to share their preferences (particularly given political agreement; <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Gershman & Cikara, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Lau et al., 2018)</ref> and extend this assumption to economic preferences (much as people prefer to learn from politically like-minded others even on nonpolitical tasks; <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Marks et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: A positive in-group reaction would then be more informative about how much observers themselves would value the outcome, so that the outcome is valued at a premium.

Moreover, observing positive affect from an in-group member may itself be rewarding (Park et al., 2016), and vicarious reward is stronger for others perceived as similar (Mobbs et al., 2009), which may carry over to the outcome that elicited the reaction.
text.formatted: Moreover, observing positive affect from an in-group member may itself be rewarding <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Park et al., 2016)</ref>, and vicarious reward is stronger for others perceived as similar <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Mobbs et al., 2009)</ref>, which may carry over to the outcome that elicited the reaction.

text.text: The second possibility is that the single (and noisy) inferred affect rating captures only part of what observers extract from an expression.

If other inferences, such as how desirable the outcome was for the demonstrator or how credible the reaction seemed, also differ systematically between in-group and out-group demonstrators, they may explain portions of the remaining in-group effect.

Within expression categories, we found little evidence consistent with differential weighting of inferred affect into WTP, and non-linear mappings between inferred affect and WTP left the premium essentially unchanged.

Whether the in-group valuation premium we observed is best described as a premium for positive in-group expression categories or as a steeper association across the whole range of inferred affect ultimately remains a question for designs with more finely graded expressions.
At first sight, adjacent findings from consumer research seem to contrast with the present results.

Luxury goods received higher price estimates when sales assistants or advertising models showed neutral rather than smiling faces, which could be attributed to increased social distance that neutral faces signal (Zhu et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Luxury goods received higher price estimates when sales assistants or advertising models showed neutral rather than smiling faces, which could be attributed to increased social distance that neutral faces signal <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">(Zhu et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: In these studies, however, expressions were portraits or verbal descriptions of people greeting customers or advertising a product, and not a reaction to receiving the product like in our design.
Moreover, whereas social distance or status seem relevant for the value of luxury products, they arguably play little role in the value of a monetary lottery outcome.
Participants also estimated market prices in imagined purchase scenarios (i.e., how other people would value the outcome) rather than stating their own incentive-compatible WTP.
Whether an expression raises or lowers valuation thus appears to depend on whether it reflects a response to the object and on what makes objects of that category valuable.
Several features of our design constrain the generality of our findings and point to directions for future work.
First, we operationalized group membership through political agreement, following recent work using similar manipulations (e.g., Kang et al., 2021; Vollberg & Cikara, 2024).
text.formatted: First, we operationalized group membership through political agreement, following recent work using similar manipulations (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Kang et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">Vollberg & Cikara, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Although participants perceived demonstrators who shared their opinions as political in-group members, our design cannot distinguish whether the observed effects depend on perceived group membership or on opinion similarity alone.

Future work that manipulates group membership independently of preference similarity would also help establish whether affect-based value inference is influenced by group membership more generally or specifically when group membership involves shared preferences.
Moreover, our manipulation varied preference similarity regarding political issues but did not probe opposing preferences regarding lottery outcomes.
Whether observers can learn to "reverse" affect-based value inference when demonstrators have outcome preferences opposed to their own remains a relevant open question (Schultner et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Whether observers can learn to "reverse" affect-based value inference when demonstrators have outcome preferences opposed to their own remains a relevant open question <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Schultner et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Although our design included Black and White demonstrators, we avoided operationalizing group membership through racialized features, given concerns about treating facial appearance as a direct indicator of racial categories (Martinez, 2025).
text.formatted: Although our design included Black and White demonstrators, we avoided operationalizing group membership through racialized features, given concerns about treating facial appearance as a direct indicator of racial categories <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Martinez, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Nevertheless, political positions, race and gender may interplay, particularly given evidence that race and gender can influence emotion perception (Craig & Lipp, 2018; Halberstadt et al., 2022; Summerell et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Nevertheless, political positions, race and gender may interplay, particularly given evidence that race and gender can influence emotion perception <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Craig & Lipp, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Halberstadt et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Summerell et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Second, our experiments isolated static facial reactions as the only available cue to the value of the hidden lottery outcomes.

This allowed us to establish that observers use others' affective reactions to inform their own valuation when no other information is available, but not how strongly they rely on affective reactions when other informative cues are available.

Testing how observers integrate expressions with other sources of information is therefore a potential next step, particularly because the interpretation of emotional expressions itself is known to depend on context (Anzellotti et al., 2021; Aviezer et al., 2017; Houlihan et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Testing how observers integrate expressions with other sources of information is therefore a potential next step, particularly because the interpretation of emotional expressions itself is known to depend on context <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Anzellotti et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Aviezer et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Houlihan et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, alternative signals such as dynamic expressions (Trautmann et al., 2009), verbal affect reports (Dashti et al., 2026) or even nonaffective reports could similarly inform valuation and be influenced by group membership.
text.formatted: Moreover, alternative signals such as dynamic expressions <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">(Trautmann et al., 2009)</ref>, verbal affect reports <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Dashti et al., 2026)</ref> or even nonaffective reports could similarly inform valuation and be influenced by group membership.

text.text: Relatedly, participants were told that demonstrators reacted to their own lottery outcomes, without any information about whether their expressions were intended to communicate with observers.

Outside the laboratory, expressions may be regulated or strategically displayed (Eldesouky & English, 2023; Gross & Levenson, 1993; Teoh & Hutcherson, 2025), and observers respond differently to expressions perceived as inauthentic (Côté et al., 2013; Hideg & van Kleef, 2017).
text.formatted: Outside the laboratory, expressions may be regulated or strategically displayed <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Eldesouky & English, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Gross & Levenson, 1993;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Teoh & Hutcherson, 2025)</ref>, and observers respond differently to expressions perceived as inauthentic <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Côté et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Hideg & van Kleef, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Such communicative intentions likely influence affect-based value inference, and how they do so remains an open question.

Across three preregistered experiments, observers used others' affective reactions to inform their valuation of hidden outcomes and were willing to pay more for outcomes associated with happy expressions and less for outcomes associated with angry expressions.
Group membership, operationalized via political agreement, changed this affect-based value inference.
Happy reactions increased WTP more when they came from an in-group member, whereas angry reactions showed no evidence of a corresponding group difference.
Observers attributed more positive affect to in-group reactions, but this accounted for only part of their larger effect on valuation.

Our results reveal how affect can substitute for missing information when outcomes are private but reactions are public, influencing economic valuation differently depending on social group membership.
Taken together, these data point to affect as one route by which preferences may spread differently within identity-aligned groups.
